title: Etta and Pecan's Starry Surprise
markdown:
Once, on a soft rolling hillside where the grass smelled like sunshine and sleepy bumblebees hummed gentle tunes, lived Etta the ewe and Pecan the porcupine. Etta was a wonderfully fluffy ball of wool, so white she looked like a cloud resting on the grass. Her eyes were wide and curious, always looking up. Every day she stood on her favourite grassy spot, nose twitching, and gazed at the big blue sky. She loved watching the clouds drift by like lazy sheep, but most of all she loved the stars that twinkled like tiny diamonds. “Oh, if only I could gather just one of those shiny stars,” she would sigh, wool puffing with a special wish. She imagined holding one, feeling its warmth and sparkle.

Pecan lived in a cosy burrow tucked beneath the sturdy roots of an old whispering oak. His quills, which looked sharp when he was surprised, were soft and tucked in when he was calm, as soft as dandelion fluff ready to fly. He spent his days carefully arranging smooth colourful pebbles and perfectly shaped fallen leaves just outside his home. He liked quiet afternoons, the rustle of wind, the chirp of crickets. He was a very good listener, especially to Etta’s starry wishes. He would tilt his head, whiskers twitching, as she described the constellations.

One day, as the sun began to set, painting the sky warm orange and soft pink, Etta gasped, a happy little sound. “Look, Pecan. Look.” A tiny point of light, brighter than the other evening stars just beginning to appear, shimmered and then, ever so gently, drifted downwards, landing with a silent whisper near the plumpest berry bushes at the edge of the meadow. “It’s a star. A real fallen star.” Her little hooves tapped a joyful rhythm. Her heart did a little dance.

She could not resist. Her heart thumped like a little drum against her woolly ribs. “I’m going to go and get it, Pecan.” Pecan, who had just finished a particularly lovely arrangement of shiny dark acorns, looked up. He was not usually one for chasing falling lights, but he knew Etta would be happiest with a friend beside her. “I’ll come with you. Just be careful where you step.”

They trotted toward the berry bushes, Etta’s nose leading, Pecan navigating the dewy grass, quills making a gentle rustle like a whisper behind her. They searched behind the plumpest juiciest bushes, leaves like tiny green umbrellas, and under the biggest soft dark leaves. Etta peered and peeked. Pecan, with gentle nudges, pushed aside a large waxy leaf with his nose. “Is this it?”

There, nestled on the dark soft earth, was not a bright shimmering star as Etta had imagined, but something even more wondrous. A cluster of delicate luminous petals, so incredibly soft they looked like captured moonlight that had decided to rest on the ground. They glowed with a gentle warm light, like tiny lanterns lit by fireflies. They were not stars from the sky, it was true, but they filled the little clearing with a soft otherworldly glow. Etta felt a tiny wobble of disappointment, a small sigh caught in her wool. Pecan saw the droop and nudged her. “They’re beautiful, Etta. They would make our supper table look so, so pretty.”

Her eyes lit up again. A quiet cosy supper with beautiful decorations would be even better than a single distant star. They carefully gathered the glowing petals, piled them into Etta’s soft woolly arms, extra gentle so as not to prick Pecan’s tender nose. The petals felt cool and wonderfully smooth, like soft silk. They carried their treasure back, the light seeming to guide their way.

At Etta’s cosy little pen, warm as a freshly baked cookie, they scattered the petals over their small wooden table, like a gentle snowfall of light. The glow made their simple supper of sweet juicy clover and shimmering dewdrops look like a feast fit for moonbeams. The scent of the petals filled the air, like dreams and moonlit gardens. They looked at each other, eyes reflecting the gentle light, and smiled. The only sound in the hushed evening was the soft happy munching of clover.

Etta still looked up at the stars that night. She also looked at the table. The petals were still glowing, a little softer now, as if they too were getting sleepy. Pecan arranged one last leaf beside the plates, just so, and neither of them wished the star back into the sky.
